title: Leestown
summary: In 1773 the McAfee company and Hancock Taylor surveyed a Kentucky River buffalo crossing north of today’s Frankfort, where Leestown was planted in 1775.
bodyMarkdown:
Leestown was the first community in what became Franklin County. It stood on the Kentucky River about a mile north of present-day Frankfort, where a buffalo trace crossed the river. Today the site lies inside Frankfort's city limits, at the entrance to Buffalo Trace Distillery.

## A crossing for buffalo and surveyors

The McAfee company and [Hancock Taylor](/stories/hancock-taylor-fincastle-surveyor/) surveyed the [Leestown](https://history.ky.gov/markers/leestown) area in 1773. Early explorers used the spot as a [hunting camp](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/423) because game was plentiful and large buffalo herds forded the river there. The McAfee brothers later founded [McAfee Station on the Salt River](/stories/mcafee-station-on-the-salt-river/).

## The Lee brothers

Two surveyors from Virginia, the brothers Hancock and Willis Lee, came to the site in the summer of 1775 and named the settlement for their family. It was the [first Anglo-American settlement](https://grokipedia.com/page/leestown,_kentucky) on the north side of the Kentucky River. The Virginia legislature formally recognized the town in 1776.

## Abandoned and rebuilt

Kentucky was a battleground during the American Revolution, and Native nations allied with the British fought to drive settlers out. Those attacks forced the settlers to leave Leestown in 1777. Hancock Lee was [killed](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/507) by Native warriors that year and the town was almost empty for a time.

Settlers came back, and by statehood in 1792 a small population was well established. Hancock Lee had willed his nephew, Willis Atwell Lee, an acre at Leestown. In the 1790s the younger Lee built a double log cabin there and called it Glen Willis. A brick house replaced it in 1815, and it still stands.

## River port

The river made Leestown a shipping point. It became a well-known port sending tobacco, hemp, corn and whiskey to New Orleans. In 1783 the Virginia General Assembly set up a tobacco inspection warehouse there, and a hemp factory ran for many years.

Leestown served as a [War of 1812 supply base](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/81) for Kentucky soldiers. It was once a commercial center and a contender for the state capital. In 1827 stone for the Old State House was quarried from the riverbank nearby.

## From Leestown to Buffalo Trace

The first distillery at Leestown opened in 1857, using a local spring and corn from central Kentucky. In 1870 it passed to [E.H. Taylor Jr.](/stories/e-h-taylor-jr-and-the-bottled-in-bond-act-1897/), who called it O.F.C. He sold it in the late 1870s to George T. Stagg. The distillery was allowed to keep producing during Prohibition, and after Prohibition Albert Blanton ran it and promoted single-barrel bourbon.

## Kentucky today

The Leestown distillery survived the 1937 flood and many changes in the liquor trade. It was renamed Buffalo Trace in 1999. Kentucky Historical Marker 103 stands at its entrance and recalls the early river town.
